title: A Field Guide to Zoo Photography
excerpt: Fences, glass, crowds and harsh sun: practical ways to make honest wildlife pictures where the animals are close but the conditions are not ideal.
author: Mono Chromattic
imageCaption: Penguins at the mouth of their burrow.
content:
## Work with the constraints

A zoo is a good place to practise wildlife technique: the animals are predictable, the light is the hard part.

### Settings that worked

| Subject | Aperture | Shutter | Focal length |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Penguins | f/6.3 | 1/500 s | about 150 mm |
| Soaring bird | f/8 | 1/800 s | 300 mm |
| Dragonfly | f/8 | 1/500 s | 300 mm |
| Pelicans | f/8 | 1/1250 s | about 64 mm |

### Rules of thumb

1. **Get close to the fence.** A wide aperture and a lens pressed near the wire makes it vanish.
2. **Shoot at eye level** with the animal whenever you can.
3. **Include the habitat.** A bit of rock, water or foliage tells the viewer where they are.
4. **Be patient.** Wait for the head to turn.

blocks.caption: A dragonfly on a stone ledge.
blocks.text: Not every subject needs a big lens. Dragonflies often sit still on a favourite perch, which lets you stay at a respectful distance and still fill the frame.
Good wildlife pictures are mostly about waiting well.
